overview: Docket (1940-41) on Japanese telegraph controls: Imperial Telegraphs absorbing Great Northern's China traffic, coded-message restrictions, and Western Union notices detailing empire-wide censorship rules on codes, languages, and radio.

people.name: Joseph C. Grew
people.role: U.S. Ambassador to Japan; sender identified in the cross-reference sheets

people.name: Francis Colt de Wolf
people.role: State Department official and recipient of the Western Union telegrams

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Great Northern cable traffic to China
subfiles.about: Records that the Imperial Japanese Telegraphs would cease accepting China-bound cable messages formerly carried by the Great Northern Telegraph Company after January 1, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Imperial Japanese Telegraphs took over Great Northern's China cable business from 1941.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on coded telegrams sent abroad from Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram containing information about sending coded telegrams from Japan to foreign destinations.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Grew's 1941 telegram concerns restrictions on sending coded telegrams abroad from Japan.

subfiles.title: Western Union notice extending Japanese censorship throughout the empire
subfiles.from: B. R. Allen, Western Union Telegraph Company
subfiles.to: Francis Colt de Wolf, State Department
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese telegraph censorship restrictions also applied to messages addressed to Korea, Taiwan, and every other part of the Japanese Empire.
subfiles.summary: Western Union reports Japan's telegraph censorship extended to Korea, Taiwan, and the rest of its empire.

subfiles.title: Western Union telegram detailing Japanese restrictions on coded and radio messages
subfiles.about: Sets out Japanese rules restricting coded telegrams, permissible languages and codes, addressing and signature practices, reply-paid messages, and mobile radio service.
subfiles.summary: Western Union details Japan's 1941 rules: coded telegrams limited to four cities, plain-language elsewhere, and radio to mobile stations suspended.

interest: Shows Japan's 1940-41 tightening of international telegraph censorship, down to specific code and language rules.
